events.text: You have lit half the south and you have never once been kept. Flying north in the hard part of winter, you look down at the dark roofs, and under each of them is one red point, banked in ash, that someone will get up in the cold to see to. You could fit. You would have to be the size of a grain of rice, in a draught, with no wings at all.

choices.text: Fold up, and go down a flue

effects.log: You come down through a great deal of soot and land in somebody's ashes, smaller than you have been since you hatched. It is very undignified. You do it again the next night.

choices.text: No. A spark is what dies when someone opens a door

effects.log: You fly on. Behind you the little red points go on being looked after by other people. You have a summer to see to.

events.text: The first hearth you try belongs to a great house, with a brass fire jar and a kitchen girl who hates it. She rakes it the way one combs a dog one means to sell. You sit in the coals and watch how it is done: oak charcoal, ash a finger thick, the lid not quite down. You have been fire since before there were kitchens, and nobody ever told you there was a right way to go to sleep.

choices.text: Stay a season, and learn to bank

effects.log: You get it wrong for most of a winter, and you have it by the thaw. A finger of ash, and breathe from the bottom. It is like being told to whisper by someone who has never heard you shout.

choices.text: Flare, and give the poor girl one warm night

effects.log: She wakes to a kitchen the colour of a sunset, screams, and throws the dishwater. You leave by the flue, hissing, with rather less dignity than you came in with.

events.text: Snow, and a lane with no lights. Someone is going from back door to back door with a fire jar under a shawl, knocking very softly, because the fire in that house died in the night and nobody must know. A house whose fire dies has told the whole village what it is. The first door stays shut. So does the second. You have burned cities, and you had no idea that one small coal could cost this much.

choices.text: Go down the dead flue, and be there when they get home

effects.log: There is a red coal in the cold ash when the jar comes back empty. Whoever it is kneels down in the dark, looks at it, and says nothing to anyone, ever. It is the first secret that you have been in.

choices.text: Follow, and see who opens

effects.log: At the fifth door an old man hands out one coal in the tongs, looking hard the other way, as one looks away from a torn coat. You go home thinking about that. You may have been doing fire wrong.

events.text: A very old cat lives on the hearth of the third house. You come down the flue with some idea of looking about. It opens one eye, considers the Bird of the South, and sits on you. It is heavy and it smells of fish. You have turned back armies. The house is asleep, the ash is warm, and you understand that as far as this animal is concerned you were put here for its benefit.

choices.text: Bear it till morning

effects.log: You burn very low and very even under a cat all night. It purrs, in a rusty way. In the morning the kitchen is exactly warm enough, and you are absurdly proud.

choices.text: Singe its tail, just a little

effects.log: It gets up without haste and walks off with its back to you. It does not come back. The kitchen smells of burnt cat until spring, and you have the strong impression that you lost.

events.text: In this kitchen the fire seed has come down from keeper to keeper for longer than the roof, mostly brides, and now it has come to {npc}, who has no one. Old Madam Seo tests the ash each morning with a poker. If it is ever cold, {npc} goes back where {he} came from. {He} banks it at night with {his} bare fingers, and talks to it, low. "Do not die," {he} says. "Not for Madam Seo. I have got used to you."

choices.text: Burn a little brighter, just under the ash

effects.log: {He} stops with {his} hand in the air, and looks at the ash. Then {he} goes on as if nothing had happened. At dawn the water is set out a little closer.

choices.text: Go back up the flue. You have no business being got used to

effects.log: You go. That fire seed stays a perfectly ordinary coal. It never goes out, because {npc} is very careful, and nobody in that house ever says so.

events.text: Madam Seo comes every morning with the poker, and has a wrist like a tax collector. In it goes, twice, and the tip is looked at. If it is red there is a grunt, and that is the highest honour this house has. You have been lying deep this week, for the pleasure of it. {npc} stands behind Madam Seo with {his} hands in {his} sleeves and {his} eyes on the ash. {He} has not eaten yet. {He} is not breathing much either.

choices.text: Come up and meet the poker

effects.log: The tip comes out red as a pepper. Madam Seo grunts. {npc} goes to the well and stands there with the bucket, not doing anything with it. You find that you would do that again for no reason.

choices.text: Stay down a little longer, to see what happens

effects.log: Madam Seo calls the whole house. {npc} goes down on {his} knees and digs in the ash with {his} fingers, and you come up under them too fast. {He} wraps the burn in a rag and says thank you to the fire. You do not know where to put yourself.

events.text: You have never been cold, so you have been studying it. It seems to start at the feet. {npc} sits up mending in the last of the night with {his} feet in the ash pan and {his} knuckles split, and this is apparently not a complaint. "You have no idea," {he} tells the fire, quite pleasantly. You really do not. You have all the heat in the south, and you are trying to work out how much one person is.

choices.text: Send the whole flue under the floor, all night

effects.log: The floor is a griddle by midnight. {He} wakes to a scorched quilt and a house full of coughing, and {he} laughs till {he} has to sit down. You have not heard that before. Madam Seo counts the firewood, twice.

choices.text: Warm one stone, the size of one foot

effects.log: {He} looks down. After a bit {he} moves the other foot over, next to it. Neither of you says anything. It is the longest conversation you have ever had.

events.text: Every dawn a bowl of clean water goes on the ledge above the hearth, for Jowang, the god of the stove. It has been done in this kitchen since there was one. This dawn {npc} sets down the god's, and then, without looking round, a second bowl, on the hearthstone, close enough to the coals to steam. {He} says nothing. {He} goes out to the well. Water is the one thing that has ever hurt you.

choices.text: Let it steam, and be empty by dusk

effects.log: It takes all day, and you are very careful. At dusk it is dry. {He} picks it up, looks in, rinses it, and at dawn it is full again. That is the whole of the ceremony, and it goes on for years.

choices.text: Spit a coal, and crack it. You cannot be owed water

effects.log: It goes with a small flat sound. {He} sweeps up the pieces. At dawn there is one bowl on the ledge, the god's, and the ash is banked as well as ever. {He} does not talk to it now.

events.text: The rice has caught, three mornings running. A voice comes from the ledge above you, about as big as a cricket. "You are burning out of turn," says Jowang. "This is a kitchen. There is one pot, and it is mine." You have been told off by the wind and by the Dragon of the East. This is somehow worse. You have been pleased, that is all. {npc} is out there scraping the pot, and {his} shoulders are shaking.

choices.text: Bow, and turn yourself down

effects.log: You get the rice right after that. The small voice says nothing further, which appears to be its way of saying well done. You have a new superior, and it lives on a shelf.

choices.text: Keep being pleased

effects.log: The crust comes up brown and thick. The small ones of the house fight over it with spoons. Madam Seo eats a bowl of it alone by the door. It becomes what that house is known for, and the ledge has gone very quiet.

events.text: A wet week at the bad end of the year, and half the hearths in the lane are dead. They come after dark, with jars under their coats. Giving fire out of a house takes the luck with it, says Madam Seo, who has the door bar in both hands. {npc} stands between Madam Seo and the door with the tongs. {He} looks at the fire. It is a very odd thing, to be asked. You have only ever happened.

choices.text: Let {him} take you, coal by coal

effects.log: Out you go, in bits, down the whole lane. By morning thirty kitchens smell of the same oak, and you are a good deal thinner. Madam Seo says that you will all be sorry. Madam Seo is wrong, and never forgives that.

choices.text: Sink low. A fire seed belongs to one house

effects.log: {He} looks at the coals, and puts down the tongs. The knocking goes on for a little, very politely. You lie in the ash and learn just what a shut door sounds like from the warm side.

events.text: It is the longest night. {npc} has flung red-bean porridge on the gate, and there is still something at the ash pan. It is thin and cold and very old. It is somebody's great-aunt, who died in a bad winter and would like to get warm. {npc} cannot see it, and {he} has started a cough. All of the red in the world is your colour. You could stand up and shine, and that would be the end of the great-aunt.

choices.text: Stand up. Red, all the way to the rafters

effects.log: It goes out at the crack of the door like breath on a cold day. The cough is gone in a week. There is a patch of kitchen floor that stays cold for good, and the cat walks around it.

choices.text: Let the great-aunt sit. It is only one night

effects.log: You have never asked any feet whose they were. In the morning the great-aunt is gone, warmed through, and {npc} coughs until the thaw. {He} would be angry, if you could find a way to tell {him}.

events.text: The south wants you. There is a coast with no beacon, and a summer that will not start itself, and every fire you ever gave is pulling at you like a small hand at a sleeve. You have stayed too long in one kitchen. If you go, the coal is only a coal, and it may die some wet night, and {npc} will be out in the lane with a jar. The fire must not go out. That is the only rule there is.

choices.text: Stay. Let the coast look after itself

effects.log: Something goes dark a long way off. You do not look. In the morning the poker comes out red, and {npc} sets out the water, and the whole of you tastes of ash.

choices.text: Stand up in the hearth one night, all of you, and show {him}

effects.log: Only for a breath, before it would take the roof. {He} sits with {his} sewing in {his} lap and the whole wall red. "I have been cooking on that," {he} says. And then: "Go, then, and come back. I can keep a fire. I kept it before you."

choices.text: Leave a plain coal behind, banked well, and go for good

effects.log: You make it the best coal you can. It has nothing in it at all. {He} will get up to it in the cold for forty more years. {He} sets out the second bowl for a while, and then {he} stops.

events.text: Madam Seo is old, and hard with it, and today the soy jar broke. You hear the poker come down across {npc}'s arm, once. You do not decide anything. You are halfway up the wall. There is thatch over you, dry as a bad year, and you have the whole house in your mouth, with everybody in it. You had forgotten what you are. It is remarkably easy to remember.

choices.text: Swallow it. All of it, back down the hearth

effects.log: It hurts more than anything has since you were an egg. One rafter is black. Madam Seo looks at it for a long time, and at the fire, and next dawn Madam Seo sets a bowl on the hearth in person, with a hand that shakes. The poker stays on its hook.

choices.text: Speak. Once, in the crackle, in the only voice you have

effects.log: You say {his} name. It sounds like a green log. {He} stands in the smoke, holding {his} arm, and looks you in whatever it is, and says: "Get down from there." You get down. You have never been so glad to be told.

choices.text: Take the kitchen. Then go, while you can still stop

effects.log: Nobody dies. The house stands in the lane with its mouth open, and {npc} is holding the empty fire jar in both hands. There is nothing left to bank. Neither of you has anywhere to go, and only one of you can fly.

events.text: There is a child by that hearth: {bk_child}, born on the worst night of the year, with the door frozen shut and the midwife cursing, on the warm stones because there was nowhere warmer. The midwife counts the fingers and then holds the feet for rather a long time. They are pink. It is cold enough in the yard to split a jar. {npc} looks at the feet, and over at the fire-hole, at you, and does not say a word.

choices.text: Burn steady. That is all anyone wants from you

effects.log: You burn steady all that night and the next. You have had a whole province at your feet. Nobody has ever been so tired, or done so little.

choices.text: Lean out of the fire-hole and look

effects.log: It is very small and very angry. It turns its head and looks straight into the coals, as nobody does, with no squint at all. You go back in, feeling that you have been seen by a magistrate.

events.text: {bk_child} can crawl now, and every soul in this house has been told that the fire-hole is the one place crawling must not go. {npc} has gone to the well. {bk_child} has seen you, and is coming across the floor at a good speed, with great purpose and one hand out. You have about a breath. You have never had to think about which way to go. You have only ever gone out.

choices.text: Pull every flame to the back, and cool the stone

effects.log: The hand pats the stone and finds it dull. {bk_child} is very let down. {npc} comes in, and sees, and drops the bucket, and it is some time before you feel able to come forward again.

choices.text: Let the edge of it be felt. Only the edge

effects.log: One small red mark, and an enormous noise. {npc} has the hand in cold water before you have finished being sorry. {bk_child} keeps clear of the fire-hole for a year. It is what a fire is supposed to teach, and you hate that.

events.text: {bk_child}, who is seven, comes hopping into the kitchen one frosty morning, on one foot and then the other, complaining bitterly about the floor. You have waited seven years for this to mean something. Then a finger gets burned on the pot handle, there are tears, and {bk_love} comes with a rag and cold water. They are cold feet. They are perfectly good ones. You sink down a little in the ash.

choices.text: Be glad, and let the child be cold

effects.log: A kitchen is somewhere to run to, out of the cold. You suppose that only works if they are cold to begin with. You burn on, and you find that this is a thing you can bear.

choices.text: Warm the step anyway, where those feet stop

effects.log: It is only one stone. It changes nothing, and the cat has it by noon. {bk_love} glances at the fire-hole on the way past, and the glance says that this is fooling nobody.

events.text: You were away one night, on the bird's business. You come down the flue at dawn to black soup: the rain got in, and nine generations have drowned. {bk_love} has been on hands and knees at it since midnight. And yet there is fire. {bk_child}, who is seven, is squatting in the fire-hole in a wet shirt, breathing into cupped hands, as one does with a chick. There is a coal in them. It did not come from anywhere.

choices.text: Go down, and sit in those hands

effects.log: You go in as small as you have ever been. The child looks at you, unsurprised, and tips you very carefully in among the kindling. {bk_love} sits back on the floor, black to the elbows, and starts to laugh, and stops. The blood will keep its own fires now, after you.

choices.text: Stay up on the beam. Let the fire be theirs

effects.log: You watch it catch from up there, with nothing to do with you at all. The poker comes out red that morning. Nobody will ever know that the line broke, or what it was mended with. You know, and it makes you feel very old.

events.text: {npc} is slow to the kitchen these days, and the bowl is late, and water reaches the floor before it reaches the hearth. {His} hands will not close on the tongs. A young one is learning the ash, badly, with {npc} on a stool giving orders. When they have gone {he} puts {his} feet to the fire-hole. "Fifty years you have kept me warm," {he} says. "And I have had a bad back for all of them."

choices.text: Burn so low and so easy that one hand could bank you

effects.log: You have never been so little trouble. {He} does it by touch, with two fingers, telling you what is wrong with the young one. All that winter you are the best-behaved fire in the kingdom.

choices.text: Get under {his} floor, and stay there all winter

effects.log: The house is through its wood by the new year, and the young one stares at the stack. {He} sleeps till morning for the first time since you have known {him}. The back is no better. {He} complains of that, warmly.

events.text: They take {bk_love} out by the back, past the soy jars, early, with frost on the mats. The young keeper has been up since before that. The bowl goes down on the hearthstone, an inch to the left of where it has been for fifty years. Nobody in the whole world would notice. There is rice to cook for forty mourners, and the one rule is that the fire does not go out.

choices.text: Burn. Just as usual, just as well

effects.log: It is the hardest thing you have done. The rice comes out exactly right. People say so, and ask for more, and you sit in the ash and let them.

choices.text: Stand up once in the hearth, all the way to the beam

effects.log: Only a breath. Every roof tile on that house is warm at the burial, with frost on all the rest, and the mourners stop talking. Then you go down. The bowl is still an inch to the left. You are told that one gets used to that.

events.text: Eighty years on, and they have a cart. {bk_child}'s people are moving to the county town, and the fire seed goes too, in a jar on somebody's knees, under a wet sack, with a great deal of bad language. The one who carries it has a flint in a sleeve. "We could just strike a light when we get there," they say. "Nobody would know." You are in the jar. You would know. So, oddly, would the jar.

choices.text: Stay lit, over every rut

effects.log: It takes nine days, and you arrive in a strange kitchen with a strange smell. The flint goes back in the sleeve. They still set out the bowl there, and they have no idea for whom.

choices.text: Go down to almost nothing, and let them worry

effects.log: They stop the cart in the rain on the third day and huddle over you with their coats spread, all of them, swearing. You come back up slowly. You had wanted to see that, and you are a little ashamed.

events.text: The swallows bring it to you: a camp in the north, in the worst of a bad winter, with the cold getting into every tent but one. Everyone has come to sit in that one, and they could not tell you why. There is a soldier in there of {bk_child}'s blood, five lives on, with a bad temper and no coat, asking them all to stop crowding. Their boots are in their pack, quite dry. They have not noticed.

choices.text: Send a week of summer north, far out of season

effects.log: It thaws one valley, and it costs you more than you would tell anyone. The army says that it was a miracle. The soldier says that it was about time.

choices.text: Leave them to it. They can keep a tent warm

effects.log: They can. You hear in spring how many came home out of that tent, and you go and sit on a hill for a bit, feeling like someone who has been paid back.

events.text: You have stayed out of kitchens for years. But there is one at the end of a lane with its fire a week dead, and {npc} sits in front of it on an upturned pail, with a jar. {He} has not gone out with it. "I will not knock," {he} says, when you come down the flue with nothing to land in. "I know what the story says you are. It says that you stay until you burn something. Well. There is plenty of room."

choices.text: Settle in the dead ash, and tell {him} everything, in the crackle

effects.log: It takes till light, and you lose your place twice. {He} gets up, stiffly, comes back with a bowl of water, looks at you, and sets it down a good way off. "To begin with," {he} says.

choices.text: Go back up. Let {him} knock at someone's door

effects.log: {He} does, in the end, at the thaw. You see the smoke from a long way off on your way south. It is somebody else's coal, and it is doing a perfectly good job.

events.text: You are asleep in the hearth of an inn, a long way south, when someone sits down at the fire-hole, unwinds their foot-cloths, and puts two long bare feet up to you. It is snowing in the yard. They are not cold feet. "I was told that you would want to see them," they say to the fire. "I walked the last part without shoes, to be sure. There is a bowl in my bag. It has been through a lot." They are laughing a little.

choices.text: Lean out to them, and let the whole room see

effects.log: Every flame in the inn bends over. The cook drops a ladle. They put out one finger, and you touch it, and it hurts neither of you. They fill the bowl before they go.

choices.text: Burn like a good kitchen fire. No one is owed a show

effects.log: You burn. They sit there until they are dry, looking at you with great satisfaction, and they set the bowl on the hearthstone. At dawn it is empty, and so is the bench.

events.text: It has snowed all night, and you go out barefoot to look for the cat, because you forgot, and it is not cold. When you come back {npc} is in the yard, looking at your tracks. They go to the gate and back, and in each one the snow has gone, right down to black earth, with a little steam. {He} does not say anything for a bit. {He} fetches the broom, and starts at the gate.

choices.text: Ask {him} why {he} is sweeping them

effects.log: "So that you do not trip," says {npc}, which is an odd worry to have about a footprint. You watch {him} do every one. You keep that for a long time, and you start to look at other people's.

choices.text: Put your straw shoes on, and say that it is cold

effects.log: You stand and shiver at {him}. You have seen it done. {npc} nods, the way one nods at a small person doing sums, and says that you are getting better at that.

events.text: People move along benches to you. You have noticed. The old men at the well end up on your side, babies stop crying when they are handed to you, and the cats of three houses have come to some arrangement. At lessons the teacher's lamp leans your way in still air. The teacher looks at it, and at you, and moves the lamp. It leans. {npc}, who brought you, is looking at the ceiling with great care.

choices.text: Sit up at the front, then. It is warmer for everybody

effects.log: They are all very fond of you by winter, in a way they could not explain. The teacher gives you the cold seat by the door, and it is warm by noon, and the teacher sighs.

choices.text: Take the place in the draught, from now on

effects.log: You learn to sit in the draught with your hands in your sleeves, and the flame stands up straight. It is hard work being ordinary. Nobody has told you that the others do not have to try.

events.text: A small one in the Gim house has been going cold for a month, though the floor is hot and the shaman has been twice. You only went in with the eggs. It is in the room, whatever it is: thin, sitting on the chest. It looks up at you, all the hair on your neck lifts, and it looks very much less sure of itself. The small one breathes out. The grandmother has seen that, and she is looking at your hands.

choices.text: Sit down by the mat, and stay till morning

effects.log: It has left by dawn. The Gims send over a whole dried fish, and there is talk, the kind with a respectful side. {npc} eats the fish, and says that you should have gone home with the eggs.

choices.text: Put down the eggs and go home

effects.log: You go quickly. You hear in a week that the small one is worse, and in a month that it is better, by some other means. You could not say what you would have done if it had gone the other way.

events.text: The dog days of your sixteenth summer, and a fever that is not a fever. The well bucket steams when you lift it. You lie down behind the barn to get out of the sun, and you wake in a ring of yellow grass with the crickets gone silent. {npc} empties a bucket over you, then sits down with a grunt. "The fire in the kitchen," {he} says, "has not been out in nine generations. There is a reason. Will you hear it?"

choices.text: Hear all of it

effects.log: A spark, a flue, a bowl of water, a child called {bk_line} with warm feet. And the one who came down: {bk_anc}. {npc} tells it like a recipe, and you sit steaming. You understand about the sweeping now.

choices.text: Say that you have a fever, and it will pass

effects.log: "It will," says {npc}. "Until next summer." {He} goes off for another bucket. You move to the cold room that night, and lie awake listening to the cat walk up and down outside the door.

events.text: Nobody's fire goes out on your lane, and it has been noticed. Grandmothers send for you now, on one excuse or another. You carry the jar at weddings. You are given a stool in the kitchens of new brides, and rice, and a long look. {npc} says that this is how it starts. They are very kind. {He} says that a village can be kind to a stove, and then there comes a year when it matters whose stove it is.

choices.text: Go and sit. It does them good

effects.log: You have a very full year, and you are owed rice in eleven houses. A bride in the Bak house cries on your shoulder, quite hot, and tells you about the household. You did not ask.

choices.text: Send your regrets, and a basket of good oak

effects.log: It burns just as well, they tell you, a little coldly. The stool is gone on your next visit. You have your evenings back, and you are not sure what to do in them.

events.text: Market day in the sixth month, and the dried-fish man has cheated you by a hand's weight. You say so. The fish man says something about your people. It takes about as long as that. You walk away with your ears ringing, and behind you the awning has caught, and someone is shouting for water. Nobody saw you do anything. You did not see you do anything. {npc}, at your elbow, looks at your hands. They are very red.

choices.text: Go back, help put it out, and pay for the cloth

effects.log: The fish man takes your silver, quite baffled, and thanks you. {npc} says on the way home that the trouble with a fire is not the time you let it out. It is the time you do not feel it go.

choices.text: Keep walking. The weight was short

effects.log: It takes two stalls with it, and no one is hurt. You sleep badly in the cold room, and in the morning you go to {npc} and ask how it is that one counts to ten.

events.text: A woman from the next county is at the gate with a basket, after a very poor night's sleep. It is the back room of the house. It has been cold there since the funeral, and things get moved. The red-bean porridge did nothing. The woman has heard, never mind how, that you need only stand in it. {npc} goes on plucking the hen. "Eat nothing there," {he} says, "and do not stay till they start to expect it."

choices.text: Go, and stand there. Just be warm at it

effects.log: It takes one night and a good deal of yawning. In the morning the room is only a room, and something in the rafters has left, not happy. You are now known in two counties, which is one more than you wanted.

choices.text: Send the woman to the shaman at the ford

effects.log: The woman goes, and does not thank you. That room stays cold another year, you hear. There are limits to how far a person can be asked to walk for a stranger, and you spend a while working out where they are.

events.text: You are up before {npc} every day of your life, and the fire is laid before {he} has opened {his} eyes, and {he} thinks that this is kindness. All winter {he} puts {his} cold feet on you in the night without asking, and you have never once flinched. Tonight {he} turns back the quilt and looks for a while at your side of the mat, where it has gone faintly brown. "How long," {he} says, "has that been happening?"

choices.text: Tell {him} about the flue, and the bowl, and the nine generations

effects.log: It takes most of the night. {He} has you hold {his} feet for all of it. At the end {he} says that it explains the cat, and the firewood, and why nobody wins an argument with you in summer, and {he} wants the warm side from now on.

choices.text: Say that it is the old quilt, and turn it over

effects.log: You turn it over. {He} lets you, and puts {his} feet back. Some time later {he} buys a new quilt, a thick one, without comment. It lasts about four years.

events.text: {npc} has gone out in the snow to see about the dog, with no shoes on, and comes back very pleased about it. You look at the tracks from the door. There is a little steam. You know what comes next: a small face looking up, one of these days, to ask why the lamps do that. There is a broom by the door. There is also a rake in the ashes, and you do remember how to bank.

choices.text: Sit {him} down at the hearth. A finger of ash, and breathe from the bottom

effects.log: You show {him} with a stick: how to bank it, how to count before speaking, when to go and stand in the cold on purpose. {He} has a very good temper by ten, and {he} scorches only the one mat.

choices.text: Get the broom. Then get {him} some shoes

effects.log: You sweep it all, down to the gate. {He} watches you do it, says nothing, and puts the shoes on. There is going to be a place behind some barn for {him}. You could draw the map.

events.text: {npc} buys red for the alchemists: cinnabar, and whatever else comes up. {He} has a long quiet face, and a copper hand-warmer that never seems to be lit. You find {him} next to you on the inn bench, holding {his} hands out a little in your direction, with {his} eyes shut. "Oh, that is very good," {he} says. "Do you know what they will give in the south for a cup of that blood? I could tell you. Sit still."

choices.text: Let {him} have it, with your hands

ok.log: {He} goes through the inn's paper door, warmer and all, and you stand over {him} till {he} has stopped smiling. {He} picks up the copper thing and looks it over for dents. {He} does not look at all like a person who has finished.

fail.log: {He} is very quick, for someone with such cold hands. You wake in the yard with something bound tight round your arm and a small neat cut inside the elbow, and a cup is missing from the inn.

choices.text: Go and sit by the door. Let your hands get cold

effects.log: It takes an hour of hard, stupid effort. You are nearly shivering. {He} opens {his} eyes, looks at the door and at you, smiles with great courtesy, and writes something in very small characters on {his} cuff.

events.text: {npc} is at the gate on the coldest night of the year, with {his} coat open and the copper warmer in {his} hands. {He} has got thin. Elixirs are hard on those who make them, {he} says, and {he} has had no feeling in {his} fingers since the harvest. {He} has a paper with a magistrate's seal, about unlicensed fire in the house. {He} would so much rather not use it. "One cup a year," {he} says. "I am only cold."

choices.text: Burn the paper in {his} hand, and then the rest of it

ok.log: The seal goes first. You drive {him} down the lane with {his} sleeve smoking, and {he} is laughing at the warmth of it, and that is what you hear in your sleep. {He} will not be back with that paper. You are not proud of how it felt.

fail.log: {He} has brought two hired men and has thought of everything, including water. You go down in the frozen yard, steaming. {He} kneels beside you a moment and warms {his} hands. There is no need for a cup, {he} says; not tonight.

choices.text: Fill the warmer from the kitchen fire, and shut the gate

effects.log: You bring it out with the tongs, a plain coal from a plain fire. {He} stands there with it in both hands, and for once {he} is not smiling. It will be out by morning. "I know," {he} says. By dawn {he} has gone.

events.text: You wake before dawn facing south. You always wake before dawn, but now it is the whole of you, like a dog at a door, and in the sixth month you cannot stay indoors. You have been up on the hill since noon with your shoes off, and the grass is going brown around you. A very large summer, a long way off, has started asking after you by name. {npc} has come up with water.

choices.text: Go south, for one season

effects.log: You walk until the rice is a different colour, and the sun is very good. You come home in autumn burnt dark and too loud, and everybody in the house steps back a little when you laugh.

choices.text: Drink the water, and go and sleep in the cold room

effects.log: It is a year of being polite to your own bones. The cat moves out. You wake before dawn, facing south, in the cold, and you turn over. You get very good at turning over.

events.text: The hill above the Bak farm is alight, in a dry autumn, with a wind behind it. Everyone is out with buckets and wet sacks, and {npc} too, at {his} age. You have stopped walking. It is a long way off, and you can feel it turn its head. It knows you. It would come to you over every roof in its road and lie down at your feet, like a big, stupid, loving thing. All you have to do is call it.

choices.text: Walk up into it, and call it home

effects.log: It takes the hill and leaves the farm. You come down at dawn with your eyebrows gone, very happy, and the people with the buckets have stopped to look at you. They do not come any closer.

choices.text: Take a bucket. Get in line like anybody

effects.log: Your arms are no use by midnight. It has the Bak farm and the two beyond before the wind changes. You sit on the wet ground with the others, and they pass you a drink. You are the only one there who knows what you could have done.

events.text: {npc} takes you to it at last: a house at the back of a valley, long fallen, with sumac growing through the roof. It was the first one. The kitchen wall still stands. {He} clears the hearthstone with {his} foot and lifts a slab, and under it there is a fire jar, with nothing to feed it for longer than anyone can reckon. You put your palm on the lid. It is warm. On the ledge is a bowl, quite dry. {bk_anc} has waited.

choices.text: Go down to the stream, and fill the bowl

effects.log: You set it on the hearthstone, close in, and you both sit until dusk, not saying anything. When you look in, it is empty, and the lid has gone a shade warmer under your hand.

choices.text: Take one coal in the tongs, and go

effects.log: It comes up red, from that cold ground. You carry it home in your own hands, and it does not burn you. {npc} looks at it, then puts the slab back very gently, as one pulls up a blanket.

events.text: It is the longest day. {npc} takes you up the sharp hill south of the town, and at noon you are both on top with no shade at all. Nothing happens for hours. Then all the heat on that hill leans in. It is very large, and it is hardly anywhere, and it has come a long way down for this, for a look at you. You know whose it is. {bk_anc} has no face to show. It is looking at your feet.

choices.text: Take off your shoes

effects.log: You stand before it barefoot on the burning rock, and it does not burn. Something goes over you like an enormous, careful breath, from the toes up, and then it is only a hot afternoon. {npc} has to sit down.

choices.text: Bow as you would to the god of the stove, and ask nothing

effects.log: You bow low, with your shoes on. It seems to find that funny, as far as a summer can. All the way home your shadow is a little too dark, and there is a warm place between your shoulders that never quite goes.

events.text: You burned a mat again last night. {npc} sits with you at the hearth, and {he} has brought the ash rake, which you may take as a comment. "A finger of ash," {he} says. "But it is not banked, is it? It is only waiting." It is true. You could let all of it go out, on purpose, as no one in your line ever has. You could stop banking it and walk south. And there is one more way. {He} knows it only by report.

choices.text: Let it go out. Learn to be cold

effects.log: There is a whole winter of cold water, the physician's needles, and the north room. In spring you borrow a coal from a neighbour, like anybody, with your feet aching, and you are wildly pleased.

choices.text: Stop banking it. Go south, and let it burn

effects.log: You leave at noon in the sixth month, by the hot road. They find your shoes at the ford. You are back sometimes for a night, when it is cold, and the whole lane sleeps well and does not ask.

choices.text: Keep it. A finger of ash, every day, for good

effects.log: It is only what the keepers have always done, and you do it to yourself. It will never be finished, and you get up to it in the cold. {npc} says that you have the hands for it.

events.text: You get chilblains. You show them to everyone. You sit in the kitchen with your feet in the ash pan like the rest of the world, and you complain, at length, with real feeling. A small one of the house brings you a coal in the tongs, and you have to blow on it three times before it catches. {npc} comes in, lays {his} cold hand on your neck to check, and leaves it there a while. "Well," {he} says.

choices.text: Learn to keep a fire, as one learns anything

effects.log: You let it die twice that winter, and you go out with the jar, ashamed, in the dark. Someone opens on the second knock. It is the best coal you have ever been given.

choices.text: Go and lie in the sun, to find out what it is like

effects.log: It is warm. It is warm from outside, and it stops when you go in. You lie there for a whole afternoon with your eyes shut, getting very slightly burnt, like a person.

events.text: The rooms do not lean any more; they empty. There is a road down the south side of the county where the grass comes up thin, and it is said that you use it. You turn up when the snow is deep, and you take a seat by the wall. People move the oil jar while you are there. {npc} still puts down a bowl for you without being asked. It steams, and {he} has started to use the thick one.

choices.text: Stay till the floors are warm, and go before they crack

effects.log: You are getting quite good at judging that. The whole lane has slept well, and there is a scorched place on the wall at the height of your shoulder. Someone has started hanging red peppers by it.

choices.text: Keep to the hills in summer, and let them have the story

effects.log: You can see the kitchen smoke from up there in the mornings, as many as you can count. Not one of them is yours, and all of them are. You have stopped trying to work out which of those you mind.

events.text: You have become a fixture. In the cold you are the one they send for when a fire has gone out and nobody must know. You come after dark by the back, with no jar, and you hold out your hands over the dead ash and you breathe. In the dog days you are up on a hill, and you are not to be spoken to. {npc} sets out a bowl at dawn, as a joke. You drink it, as a joke. It has gone on for some years.

choices.text: Go on knocking at the back doors

effects.log: You know what is wrong in every kitchen in three counties, and you will never say it. Being trusted with that is a very warm thing, and it does not scorch.

choices.text: Take a summer on the hill, and leave the keepers to it

effects.log: They manage, or they mostly do. There is a young one in the Gim house who banks better than you, and you tell {npc} so, with some bitterness.

events.text: You are old now, and you still wake first. Nobody has ever managed to get up before you to lay the fire. There is a new one in the house being taught the ash, and getting it wrong. You get down on your knees, which takes a while, and you take the rake out of those young hands. {npc} watches from the door with {his} tea. "A finger," you say. "Not that. Who taught you that?" It is the best part of your day.

choices.text: Show it once more, slowly, with your own hand

effects.log: You make them do it nine times. On the tenth they have it, and they look up to see if you noticed, and you are looking at something else. That is how it was done to you.

choices.text: Let them get it wrong, and see what the fire does

effects.log: It sulks, and it comes back by morning. They have learned more from that than you could have told them. You say that you meant it all along, and {npc} has to put down the tea.

events.text: They have brought you in to lie by the hearth, because you asked, and it is a lot of trouble with the mats. Your feet are out from under the quilt. {npc} looks at them and tucks them in, and they come out. It is not yet dawn. Someone young comes in yawning, with a bowl of clean water, and looks at the ledge, and then at you, and stands there, not sure where to put it.

choices.text: Point to the hearthstone, close in

effects.log: They set it down there. They do not ask. They will do it every morning for a long time, and tell nobody why. You lie and watch it begin to steam.

choices.text: Shake your head. The god has the ledge, and you are not thirsty

effects.log: They put it up on the ledge, as is proper. You watch the fire for a while, and it is only a kitchen fire, getting on with it. It has rice to see to. You have never been so pleased to be no trouble.
